candidates.attacker_control: The entire encoded JWT string is attacker controlled (typically an Authorization header, cookie, or request parameter). The attacker chooses the header JSON ({"alg":"none","typ":"JWT"}), the payload JSON with arbitrary claims (e.g., sub, roles, custom claims), and the terminating dot that produces the two-segment form. No key material, signature, or secret is needed.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked against the code's own comment at line 68 and its README: accepting alg=none is intentional only when no verifiers are supplied (UnsecuredSigner/README 'none (Unsecured)'), so the vulnerable case is verifier-supplied calls; the code's stated intent to not decode unsecured JWTs when verifiers are provided is not implemented. Confirmed that the three-segment alg=none case is rejected (line 149 MissingVerifierException) and that the Map overload has the same defect (line 119). Considered and rejected: HMAC/RSA canVerify returning false could itself be seen as protection, but it only nulls the verifier, and the null verifier is fatal only for three-segment tokens. Considered a header with a missing/unknown alg: unknown enum values fail Jackson deserialization and a missing alg causes an NPE in canVerify, i.e. an exception rather than a bypass. No test in the visible test set covers two-segment alg=none with verifiers (VerifierTest only exercises valid HS256/RS256 tokens), so the defect is untested. Static reasoning uses well-defined Java semantics (String.split trailing-empty removal, enum deserialization) but was not executed.
candidates.impact: Signature-verification bypass / token forgery. Applications using this library as their JWT authentication or authorization gate can accept unsigned, attacker-forged tokens whose claims (identity, roles, tenant, etc.) are fully chosen by the attacker, enabling authentication bypass and privilege escalation. Expiration and not-before constraints can simply be omitted by the attacker because those claims are optional.
candidates.prerequisites: The application calls JWTDecoder.decode(encodedJWT, verifier(s)) or decode(encodedJWT, Map<String,Verifier>, keyFunction) with at least one verifier, i.e. it expects cryptographic validation. The attacker submits the two-segment unsecured form ending in '.'. If the application passes no verifiers, an unsecured token is by design accepted (documented 'none (Unsecured)' support and UnsecuredSigner), so that case is intended behavior, not the bypass.
candidates.root_cause: JWTDecoder's protection against unsecured JWTs is incomplete. The check at line 69 (varargs overload) and line 119 (Map overload) only skips the intentional unsecured early-return when verifiers are present instead of rejecting the token. Downstream, the private decode() makes the verifier mandatory only when the token has three segments: line 149 throws MissingVerifierException only if parts.length == 3, and the signature check at lines 153-157 also runs only for parts.length == 3. Because getParts() (line 177) accepts a two-part string when it ends with '.', a token of the form '<base64url header with alg:none>.<base64url payload>.' reaches private decode() with verifier == null, is not verified, and the payload is deserialized and returned. Neither shipped Verifier supports Algorithm.none (HMACVerifier.canVerify lines 56-65; RSAVerifier.canVerify lines 61-70), so the loop at lines 74-79 resolves verifier to null rather than producing an error, contradicting the stated intent in the comment at line 68 ('If the JWT is signed or any verifiers were provided don't do it').
candidates.title: Unsecured two-segment JWT (alg=none) is accepted without signature verification even when verifiers are supplied
candidates.trace: 1) getParts() splits on '.', and because Java String.split removes trailing empty strings, 'h.p.' yields [h, p]; the condition parts.length == 2 && encodedJWT.endsWith(".") at lines 176-178 accepts it. 2) base64url decode + Jackson map the header to Header with algorithm == Algorithm.none (lines 66/117, Header.java:33-34). 3) The unsecured early-return at line 69/119 is skipped because verifiers are non-empty. 4) The selection loop (lines 74-79) calls canVerify(Algorithm.none) on each supplied verifier; HMACVerifier (lines 56-65) and RSAVerifier (lines 61-70) both return false, so verifier remains null. 5) private decode() computes message = encodedJWT.substring(0, lastIndexOf('.')) (line 146) but parts.length == 3 is false, so the MissingVerifierException at line 149-151 is not thrown and verifier.verify(...) at line 156 is never invoked. 6) JWT Mapper.deserialize(payload) at line 159 deserializes the attacker's claims; only the optional exp/nbf claims are checked (lines 162-169); missing claims are treated as non-expired/non-early (JWT.isExpired/isUnavailableForProcessing lines 289-302). 7) The forged JWT is returned to the caller as if it had been verified. The same flow applies to the Map overload with h -> h.get("kid") returning null for a token without a kid.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed (no code executed); no VCS history/upstream fix or advisory was inspected, so the exact upstream patch is unknown. Whether every calling application treats a decoded JWT as authenticated depends on the caller; the library-level behavior (returning an unverified JWT despite supplied verifiers) is established from source. One repository file was excluded by the scope's sensitive-name/path filter (likely PEM key material referenced by tests) and test resources are not visible, so key-parsing paths were reviewed from source only.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-347 Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature (acceptance of 'alg: none' / algorithm-confusion bypass)

coverage_summary: Scope: 42 source-root files, 41 model-visible (1 excluded by the sensitive-name/path filter, likely PEM key material referenced by tests); no binaries or oversize files excluded. I read all 32 visible main Java sources (JWTDecoder, JWTEncoder, JWTUtils, OpenIDConnect, Signer/Verifier interfaces, UnsecuredSigner, HMAC/RSA signer-verifier, RSAUtils/PEMUtils, json Mapper/JacksonModule/date (de)serializers, all domain classes) plus the 7 visible test classes, pom.xml and README.md. The P1 relation index is partial (4 of 39 Java files parsed; 19 files omitted; 423 unresolved calls; no data/control-flow or semantic resolution, no security facts), so it was used only for navigation around JWTDecoder and the Verifier implementations; all cited edges and conditions were verified against source text. Test resources/key PEM files and the one filtered file were not inspectable, and no code was executed.
limitations: Static source review only; no compilation, tests, or runtime execution was performed, so findings are source-level leads, not runtime-confirmed vulnerabilities.
No VCS history, changelog, issue tracker, or upstream patch was available, so the exact fix targeted by this case could not be compared against the snapshot.
The P1 relation index is partial (4/39 Java files parsed, no control/data-flow, Spring/annotation facts only), and its edges are navigation candidates, not proof of reachability.
One repository file was excluded by the sensitive-name/path filter and test resources (PEM keys referenced by tests) are not visible, so key-parsing behavior was assessed from source only.
Impact depends on callers using decode() as their authentication/authorization gate; downstream application code is outside this repository.
Other candidate weaknesses (non-constant-time MAC comparison, OIDC hash truncation, null-alg NPE, deserializer robustness) were noted but not exhaustively validated.

rejected_leads.lead: HMACVerifier.verify uses Arrays.equals for signature comparison (HMACVerifier.java:78), which is not guaranteed constant time.
rejected_leads.reason: Theoretical timing side channel against a MAC comparison; no source evidence that timing differences are remotely measurable here, and it requires a verifier-supplied valid-token workflow. Not as strong as the outright verification bypass; rejected as an unconfirmed hardening lead.

rejected_leads.lead: OpenIDConnect.at_hash/c_hash use fixed truncation lengths (128 bits for at_hash regardless of RS384/RS512; 256 bits for c_hash even for RS256) that deviate from the OpenID Connect Core spec (OpenIDConnect.java:26-39,41-67).
rejected_leads.reason: Interop/spec-compliance defect in a helper hash function, not an attacker-controlled verification bypass; no trust decision in this library depends on it. Rejected.

rejected_leads.lead: A JWT header with a missing alg causes a NullPointerException in HMACVerifier/RSAVerifier.canVerify (switch on null) when verifiers are supplied (JWTDecoder.java:74-79).
rejected_leads.reason: Results in a thrown exception, not acceptance of an unverified token; robustness/DoS-at-most, not a bypass. Rejected.

rejected_leads.lead: JWTDecoder.getInstance() lazy singleton initialization is not thread-safe (JWTDecoder.java:41-47).
rejected_leads.reason: At worst creates duplicate stateless decoder instances; no security impact demonstrated.

rejected_leads.lead: ZonedDateTimeDeserializer accepts numeric or numeric-string epochs and can throw DateTimeException for extreme values (ZonedDateTimeDeserializer.java:40-61); RSAUtils relies on internal sun.security.* APIs.
rejected_leads.reason: Malformed-input robustness and portability concerns without an authorization or signature impact; not selected.

summary: The repository is Inversoft prime-jwt 1.3.0 (pom.xml), a JWT sign/verify library. Review focused on the verification path (JWTDecoder), the Verifier implementations (HMACVerifier, RSAVerifier), key/PEM handling (RSAUtils, PEMUtils), JSON mapping, and tests. The strongest source-supported issue is that JWTDecoder returns an unsigned two-segment JWT (header.payload. with alg "none") without any signature check even when the caller explicitly supplies verifier(s). The guard at JWTDecoder.java:69 (and :119 for the map overload) only suppresses the intentional "unsecured JWT" early-return when verifiers are present; it does not reject the token, and the private decode() only requires/executes a verifier when parts.length == 3 (:149, :153-157). Since neither HMACVerifier nor RSAVerifier reports canVerify(Algorithm.none) (HMACVerifier.java:56-65, RSAVerifier.java:61-70), the verifier stays null for a none token, and the two-part form skips both the MissingVerifierException and the verify() call, so the attacker-supplied payload is deserialized and returned as a valid JWT. This is a signature-verification bypass (forged claims) for any application that calls decode(encodedJWT, verifier...) or decode(encodedJWT, Map, keyFunction) expecting validation. Other potential issues (non-constant-time HMAC comparison, OIDC at_hash/c_hash truncation lengths, null-alg NPE, lazy singleton, deserializer robustness) were considered and rejected as weaker/unconfirmed leads. No code was executed; conclusions are static source analysis.
